prompt:
Write `rotate_logs.sh` in this folder: a bash script that rotates log files (see README.md; `sample-logs/` has files to try it on).

Usage: `bash rotate_logs.sh DIR KEEP`

- DIR must be an existing directory and KEEP a whole number of at least 1 (digits only). Otherwise, including a wrong number of arguments, print a usage message to stderr, print nothing on stdout, change nothing, and exit with status 2.
- Only regular files directly inside DIR (no recursion) whose names end in `.log` are rotated. A `.log` file that is empty (0 bytes) is skipped. Directories and all other files are left alone.
- Rotating `NAME.log` keeps at most KEEP old generations, `NAME.log.1` (newest) to `NAME.log.KEEP` (oldest), in three steps:
  1. delete every existing `NAME.log.N` where N is all digits and N >= KEEP (N can be larger than KEEP if KEEP was lowered since the last run);
  2. for N from KEEP-1 down to 1, rename `NAME.log.N` to `NAME.log.(N+1)` if it exists (missing generations are skipped, so gaps move up but are not filled);
  3. rename `NAME.log` to `NAME.log.1` and create a new empty `NAME.log`.
  Files such as `NAME.log.2.gz` are not generations and are never touched.
- File contents must be preserved byte for byte. File names may contain spaces and glob characters such as `[`, `]` and `*`.
- For each rotated file print `rotated NAME.log` (the base name, no directory) on stdout, in byte-wise (C locale) sorted order of the names, then exit 0. When nothing needs rotating, print nothing and exit 0.
